chapters.title: Chapter 4: Trading Forex Legally in India

lessons.title: Exchange-Traded Currency Derivatives on NSE and BSE

children.text: Priya runs a textile export unit in Coimbatore. A US retailer will pay her $150,000 in about two months. If the rupee strengthens from 95.80 to 94.60 before the money arrives, she loses ₹1,80,000 without selling a single shirt less. Her bank offers a forward, but she wants a transparent price she can see on a screen and the option to close the hedge early. So she opens the currency segment on her broker's platform and sells USD/INR futures on NSE. This lesson shows you what is listed on India's exchanges, who may use each contract, how a position is margined and settled, and how Priya's hedge actually works rupee by rupee.

body.text: Exchange-traded currency derivatives turn a private deal with a bank into a standard, transparent contract guaranteed by a clearing corporation. For rupee pairs, they exist to hedge real currency risk, and used that way they convert an uncertain future exchange rate into a known one.

children.text: What Is Listed, and Who Can Use It

markDefs.definition: The entity that becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer on an exchange, guaranteeing settlement. NSE Clearing Ltd clears NSE trades and Indian Clearing Corporation Ltd clears BSE trades.

children.text: Currency futures and options trade in a separate currency derivatives segment on NSE and BSE, and also on the Metropolitan Stock Exchange. You access them through a SEBI-registered broker after activating the segment. Every trade is novated to a
clearing corporation
, so you never depend on the person on the other side paying up. The contracts fall into two groups with very different eligibility rules.

body.text: Brokers let you activate the currency segment with a few clicks, and no one will ask you to upload an export invoice for a small position. That convenience does not change the rule. Rupee-pair contracts may be used only to hedge a genuine exposure, and when you trade them you are confirming that such an exposure exists. If you have no currency exposure, stick to the cross-currency contracts.

children.text: The Life of a Currency Futures Position
Identify the exposure.
Priya is owed $150,000 in about two months. A stronger rupee hurts her, so she needs a position that gains when USD/INR falls: a short futures position.
Choose size and expiry.
$150,000 ÷ $1,000 = 150 lots. She picks the monthly contract that expires closest to, but not before, her expected payment date.
Post margin.
Her broker blocks initial margin plus extreme loss margin upfront, a small percentage of the contract value.
Mark to market daily.
Each evening, gains are credited and losses debited in rupees based on the day's settlement price.
Close or settle.
She can buy back the futures when the dollars arrive, or hold to expiry, when the contract is cash-settled against the reference rate.

body.title: Margin on the hedge
body.prompt: Priya sells 150 lots of USD/INR futures at 95.80. If the total margin required is 2.5% of the contract value, how much margin is blocked, in rupees?
body.explanation: Contract value = 150 lots × $1,000 × 95.80 = ₹1,43,70,000. Margin = 2.5% × ₹1,43,70,000 = ₹3,59,250. She controls a hedge on about ₹1.44 crore of receivables with about ₹3.6 lakh of margin, which is why margin must be kept topped up when the market moves against the futures.

body.title: The first evening's MTM
body.prompt: On the first day, USD/INR futures settle at 96.10, above Priya's selling price of 95.80. What is the mark-to-market debit on her 150-lot short position, in rupees?
body.explanation: Loss = (96.10 minus 95.80) × $1,000 × 150 = 0.30 × 1,50,000 = ₹45,000, debited that evening. This is not a real loss for her business: the same rupee weakness means her $150,000 receivable is now worth ₹45,000 more. A hedger must still have the cash to meet these debits, even when the underlying exposure is gaining.

children.text: How the Hedge Locks the Rate

body.caption: Priya's $150,000 receivable, hedged by selling 150 lots at 95.80 and held to expiry (ignoring costs)
S_T is the reference rate at expiry and F_0 the futures price when the hedge was placed. The spot rate cancels out.
Priya's short USD/INR futures sold at 95.80. It gains as the rupee strengthens and loses as it weakens, mirroring her receivable so that the combined result stays at 95.80.

body.title: Why real hedges are never perfectly exact

children.text: Lot rounding.
A $150,600 receivable cannot be hedged exactly with $1,000 lots. The last $600 stays unhedged.
Date mismatch.
Buyers rarely pay on the exact expiry day. If the dollars arrive a week after expiry, the rate moves in that gap are unhedged, or she must roll the position into the next month.
Basis.
If she closes the futures before expiry, the futures price will not exactly match the spot rate her bank gives her for the dollars, because it still contains some forward premium.
Costs.
Brokerage, exchange charges, GST and stamp duty, plus the bank's own spread when converting the actual dollars.

body.title: Which side for an importer?
body.question: Farooq imports machine parts into Pune and must pay a Japanese supplier's dollar invoice of $80,000 in six weeks. He wants to hedge on NSE. What should he do?
body.explanation: An importer is hurt when the rupee weakens and USD/INR rises, so he needs a position that gains when USD/INR rises: a long futures position. $80,000 ÷ $1,000 = 80 lots. Selling would double his risk, and EUR/USD does not hedge a dollar-rupee exposure.

children.text: Cross-Currency Contracts: Profit in Dollars, Paid in Rupees

Cross-currency contracts work differently. A lot is 1,000 units of the base currency, so one EUR/USD lot is €1,000. Profit or loss is calculated in the quote currency, US dollars for EUR/USD and GBP/USD, and yen for USD/JPY, and then converted into rupees using the reference rate. That creates a second, smaller currency effect: your rupee profit depends on both the pair's move and USD/INR.

body.title: A EUR/USD trade in rupees
body.prompt: Rhea buys 40 lots of EUR/USD futures on NSE at 1.1600 and sells them at 1.1650. The profit is converted to rupees at a reference rate of 95.50. What is her profit in rupees, before costs?
body.explanation: Move = 1.1650 minus 1.1600 = 0.0050, or 50 pips. Position size = 40 lots × €1,000 = €40,000. Profit in dollars = 0.0050 × 40,000 = $200. In rupees: $200 × 95.50 = ₹19,100. If USD/INR had been 94.50 on the conversion day, the same trade would have paid ₹18,900, which shows the second currency effect built into cross-currency contracts.

body.title: Designing Farooq's hedge
body.scenario: Farooq, the Pune importer, has an $80,000 payment due on 12 November. The November USD/INR futures contract expires two working days before the last business day of November, well after his payment date. The October contract expires in late October, before his payment. USD/INR October futures trade at 95.70 and November at 95.95. His accountant suggests: "Just buy 100 lots of November futures to be safe, in case the rupee really crashes."
body.prompt: Recommend how Farooq should structure the hedge: which side, how many lots, which expiry, and how to handle the date mismatch. Then evaluate the accountant's suggestion.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Side and size: buy USD/INR futures, since a weaker rupee hurts an importer. $80,000 ÷ $1,000 = 80 lots.
2. Expiry: the November contract covers his 12 November payment date. The October contract would expire before he pays, leaving the last few weeks unhedged unless he rolls it.
3. Closing: on or around 12 November, when he buys the actual dollars from his bank, he sells the 80 November futures. Because the futures still contain some forward premium at that point, the hedge will be close but not exact. That basis difference is the price of using a standard contract.
4. The cost of November over October is visible in the price, 95.95 versus 95.70, reflecting the extra time and the interest rate gap.
5. The accountant's 100 lots would hedge $100,000, which is $20,000 more than Farooq owes. The extra 20 lots have no underlying exposure. For rupee-pair contracts, that portion is speculation and not permitted, and it would also create losses with nothing to offset them if the rupee strengthens.

body.title: Before placing a hedge on NSE or BSE
steps: Write down the exposure: currency, amount, and expected payment or receipt date.
Choose the side: exporters and those receiving dollars sell USD/INR; importers and those paying dollars buy.
Convert the amount into lots and avoid hedging more than the real exposure.
Pick the expiry that covers the payment date, and plan how you will close or roll the position.
Keep cash ready for daily mark-to-market debits, not just the initial margin.
Record the hedge and the underlying invoice, so you can show the exposure if asked.

points: NSE, BSE and MSE list currency futures and options, traded through SEBI-registered brokers and guaranteed by clearing corporations.
Rupee-pair contracts are for hedging genuine currency exposures. Cross-currency contracts like EUR/USD can be traded without an exposure within exchange limits.
A USD/INR futures lot is $1,000, ticks are ₹0.0025, and contracts are cash-settled in rupees against the reference rate.
Positions need upfront margin and are marked to market daily, so hedgers need cash for interim debits even when their underlying exposure is gaining.
Exporters sell USD/INR futures and importers buy them. Held to expiry, the hedge locks in the futures price.
Real hedges are imperfect because of lot rounding, date mismatches, basis and costs.
Cross-currency profits are calculated in the quote currency and converted to rupees at the reference rate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, trading, hedging or legal advice. Contract specifications, margins, expiries and eligibility rules are set by the exchanges, SEBI and RBI and can change. Check the latest details on the NSE and BSE websites and with your broker, and consult a qualified adviser before hedging business exposures.
